tytul: Wild garlic in soy sauce: why there is no recipe here
wstep: There is no recipe here for raw wild garlic leaves pickled in soy sauce, Korean style (myeongi namul).

ostrzezenia.tekst: Almost any food that is not very acidic, with a pH above 4.6, can support the growth of Clostridium botulinum and toxin production.
According to the FDA, the minimum temperature for growth and toxin production by Clostridium botulinum type E and nonproteolytic types B and F is 38°F (3.3°C).
According to BfR, young wild garlic leaves resemble those of the poisonous lily of the valley and the very poisonous autumn crocus; when in doubt, it is better not to eat them.

According to AGES, wild garlic leaves may be contaminated with fox tapeworm eggs, which can cause a life-threatening disease in humans; the eggs survive usual freezing at -18 °C and are killed at around +60 °C.

akapity: All fresh vegetables except most tomatoes are low-acid foods with a pH above 4.6.
This pickle uses soy sauce, not vinegar.
The leaves in this pickle are raw, so they are not heated to the temperature at which, according to AGES, fox tapeworm eggs are killed.
According to AGES, wild garlic is also confused with spotted arum, Solomon’s seal and wild tulips.
JarAtlas rule: if you are not sure that every leaf is wild garlic, do not use the leaves.
This pickle is meant to be kept in the refrigerator.
JarAtlas has found no tested recipe for wild garlic in soy sauce from a checked source.
